clue.text: Marketing rep smashed cash machine, by the way

indicators.note: something smashed is broken into pieces that can be put back together in a different order

parts.note: all twelve letters of these two words are the raw material

explanation.surface: A sales representative takes out their frustration on an ATM by the roadside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cash machine' tempts you towards an ATM, but 'by the way' pins it to the roadside: a coin-fed machine on the street.
explanation.definitionFit: A parking meter is a coin-operated device standing beside the road, so it is literally a money-taking machine by the street.

clue.text: Newspapers covering ordinary women's outstanding skill

indicators.note: one thing covering another wraps around it, so the outer word encloses the inner letters

parts.note: the press is newspapers collectively
O is a standard abbreviation for ordinary
W is the abbreviation for women

explanation.surface: The papers are writing up some ordinary women's remarkable talents.
explanation.walkthrough: O and W sit together inside PRESS, splitting it as PR-OW-ESS; the 's simply links wordplay to definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Prowess means exceptional ability or expertise, a direct synonym for outstanding skill.

clue.text: Romeo, on the 15th of March say, goes on horseback

parts.note: Romeo is R in the NATO phonetic alphabet
in the Roman calendar the Ides fell on the 15th of March, with 'say' showing it is one example

explanation.surface: Romeo heads off on horseback on the Ides of March, the day Caesar was stabbed.
explanation.walkthrough: The Ides of March, the 15th, is famous as the day Julius Caesar was assassinated; 'say' tells you the date is an example of Ides.
explanation.definitionFit: To ride is to travel seated on a horse, so rides is a third-person verb matching goes on horseback.

clue.text: Pub on fire, ruined — might this ease the pain?

indicators.note: a ruined thing has lost its original shape, so the letters must be rebuilt in a new order

parts.note: nine letters of fodder taken from these three words

explanation.surface: A landlord whose pub has burned down might well reach for a painkiller.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue doubles as a scene: after your pub burns down you need something for the pain.
explanation.definitionFit: Ibuprofen is a common over-the-counter painkiller, so it is something that might relieve pain.

clue.text: Present tense introduced by image on computer

parts.note: a GIF is a common computer image file format
T is the grammatical abbreviation for tense

explanation.surface: Grammar lesson: the present tense shown with a picture on screen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Present tense' reads as one grammar phrase, but 'Present' is the definition and 'tense' is just a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A gift is something given, which is the noun sense of present.

clue.text: Leo bares wobbly bits for piercing

indicators.note: wobbly suggests something unsteady and moving about, so the letters shift into a new order

parts.note: eight letters of fodder from the name and the verb

explanation.surface: Leo strips off and shows his jiggling flesh, ready for some body piercing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wobbly bits' is a jokey phrase for flabby flesh, but 'wobbly' belongs to the wordplay and 'bits for piercing' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Earlobes are the soft lower parts of the ear, the parts most commonly pierced for earrings.

clue.text: The setter turns up on exercise yard exhausted

indicators.note: in a down entry, turning up means reading from bottom to top, so the word is written backwards

parts.note: the setter refers to themself as me
PT is physical training
Y is the abbreviation for yard

explanation.surface: The puzzle-maker arrives at the exercise yard worn out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Exercise yard' reads as one place, but it splits into two abbreviations.
explanation.definitionFit: Exhausted in the sense of used up or drained means having nothing left, so empty is a synonym.

clue.text: Message RAC about suspended traffic

parts.note: a cable is a telegram, a message sent by wire

indicators.note: about here means turned around, so the three letters are read in the opposite direction

parts.note: taken as written; the RAC is the Royal Automobile Club, a British motoring breakdown organisation

explanation.surface: A notice from the motoring organisation reports that traffic has been halted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Suspended traffic' looks like stalled roads; here it means vehicles that hang from a wire.
explanation.definitionFit: A cable car hangs from an overhead cable, so it is transport, or traffic, that is literally suspended in the air.

clue.text: Country never, ever accepting Republican!

indicators.note: to accept is to take something in, so the phrase opens up to hold the extra letter

parts.note: no way is an emphatic refusal, meaning never ever
R is the abbreviation for Republican

explanation.surface: A political cry: this country will never let a Republican in!
explanation.definitionFit: Norway is a Scandinavian nation, so it is an example of a country.

clue.text: Bumbling gent's vintage railway equipment?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a fussy, ineffectual old man
second meaning, read literally: an aged buffer, the sprung stop at the end of a railway track

explanation.walkthrough: The 's stands for 'is', joining the two meanings; the question mark flags the jokey literal reading of the second.
explanation.definitionFit: Old buffer is British slang for a doddery elderly man, and buffers are the shock-absorbing stops on railway lines.

clue.text: Joanna, Penny and Oscar embracing Ian

indicators.note: to embrace is to put your arms around, so the outer letters wrap the name

parts.note: P is the abbreviation for penny
Oscar is O in the NATO phonetic alphabet
taken as written

explanation.surface: Three friends, Joanna, Penny and Oscar, all hug Ian.
explanation.walkthrough: Joanna looks like another person in the group, but it is Cockney rhyming slang: Joanna rhymes with piano (said 'pianner').
explanation.definitionFit: In Cockney rhyming slang a joanna is a piano, so the name stands for the instrument.

clue.text: Criticised open-ended guarantee

indicators.note: open-ended means having no closed ends, so the first and last letters are removed

parts.note: to censure is to criticise formally

explanation.surface: An open-ended guarantee has come in for criticism.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Open-ended guarantee' reads as a phrase, but 'open-ended' acts on the word before it, stripping its outer letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To ensure is to make certain that something happens, which is to guarantee it.

clue.text: Robert mean about extremely dodgy damage sustained amidships?

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the name is placed around the kept letters

parts.note: Bob is a short form of Robert

indicators.note: extremely points to the extremes of the word, so only its first and last letters are kept

parts.note: the first and last letters of dodgy
low means mean or base

explanation.surface: Robert is stingy about some suspicious damage to a ship's middle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Amidships' suggests a vessel, but the question mark points to a human middle: a punch to the torso.
explanation.definitionFit: A body blow is a punch to the torso, and figuratively a severe setback; amidships playfully means the midriff.

clue.text: Close, yet unapproachable?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: airless and humid, as of weather or a room
second meaning: formal and stiff in manner

explanation.walkthrough: 'Close, yet unapproachable' sounds like a paradox about distance; 'close' means muggy, not near.
explanation.definitionFit: Stuffy describes both a stale, airless atmosphere and a starchy, aloof person who is hard to get near.

clue.text: Minicab driver finally abandons Greek superbrain

parts.note: Uber is a ride-hailing service, a modern minicab

indicators.note: to abandon is to leave behind, so that letter drops out of the following word

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: finally points to the final letter of the preceding word

parts.note: the last letter of driver

explanation.surface: A taxi driver eventually leaves behind a brilliant Greek passenger.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Minicab driver' reads as one person, but it splits: the minicab is the ride-hailing firm, and only the final letter of driver is used, as the letter that leaves the nationality.
explanation.definitionFit: An übergeek is an extreme nerd, a person of exceptional intellect in technical matters, hence a superbrain.

clue.text: Clark, mild-mannered chap, fortunate to miss the first Derby here

indicators.note: missing the first means the opening letter is left off the word

parts.note: Clark Kent is Superman's mild-mannered alter ego
lucky means fortunate

explanation.surface: Mild-mannered Clark was lucky to miss the start of the Derby.
explanation.walkthrough: Derby suggests the English horse race or city, but the Kentucky Derby is America's most famous horse race.
explanation.definitionFit: The Kentucky Derby is run every year in Louisville, so Kentucky is the US state where that Derby takes place.

clue.text: Clock magazine article?

parts.note: Time is a famous news magazine
a piece is an article in a publication

explanation.surface: A news report about clocks, or an article in Time magazine.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark hints that the whole thing also reads as a description: a piece in Time magazine.
explanation.definitionFit: A timepiece is any instrument for measuring time, such as a clock or watch.

clue.text: Writer Gustave upset Alf (wild brute!)

indicators.note: upset means knocked over and disordered, so the letters are jumbled
wild means unruly and out of control, another signal that these letters are scrambled

parts.note: three letters of fodder
five more letters of fodder

explanation.surface: The writer Gustave has offended Alf, who is a wild brute.
explanation.definitionFit: Gustave Flaubert was the French novelist who wrote Madame Bovary.

clue.text: Place for putting filly regularly being a pest in the garden

parts.note: on a golf course, putting is done on the green

indicators.note: regularly means at even intervals, so every other letter is taken

parts.note: the first, third and fifth letters of filly

explanation.surface: A young horse is wandering onto the golf green, making a nuisance of itself.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Putting' is the golf stroke, not 'placing'.
explanation.definitionFit: Greenfly are aphids, small sap-sucking insects that damage garden plants.

clue.text: Good old beer put over head of inn keeper

indicators.note: putting something over another covers it, so the beer word is spread around the single letter

parts.note: G is the abbreviation for good
O is the abbreviation for old
ale is a type of beer

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter

parts.note: the first letter of inn

explanation.surface: Some good old ale is served up at the head of an innkeeper's table.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Inn keeper' reads as a landlord; 'keeper' is the definition, a goalkeeper.
explanation.definitionFit: Goalie is the informal word for a goalkeeper, the player who guards the goal.

clue.text: Sting finally interests US intelligence

parts.note: to smart is to sting with pain

indicators.note: finally points to the final letter of the following word

parts.note: the last letter of interests

explanation.surface: Sting, the singer, ends up interesting American spies.
explanation.walkthrough: 'US intelligence' suggests the CIA; it is American slang for brains.
explanation.definitionFit: In American usage, smarts means cleverness or know-how, the brainpower sense of intelligence.

clue.text: Frank, the willing lunar astronaut?

parts.note: surface reading: a candid space traveller eager to go to the Moon; setter's reading: the singer named Frank who famously asked to be flown to the Moon in his hit song

explanation.walkthrough: Frank looks like the adjective for candid, but it is a first name; the singer recorded the standard 'Fly Me to the Moon'.
explanation.definitionFit: Frank Sinatra's best-known recordings include 'Fly Me to the Moon', making him a jokey volunteer for lunar travel.

clue.text: Sailor who got fleeced on the return voyage?

definitions.text: Sailor who got fleeced on the return voyage?

parts.words: Sailor who got fleeced on the return voyage?
parts.note: surface reading: a seaman cheated out of his money on the way home; setter's reading: one of Jason's crew, who obtained the Golden Fleece and brought it home

explanation.walkthrough: 'Fleeced' normally means swindled; in Greek myth Jason's crew sailed on the Argo to fetch the Golden Fleece.
explanation.definitionFit: The Argonauts were the heroes who sailed with Jason and carried the Golden Fleece back from Colchis.

clue.text: North American cheers leader of Lebanese province once

parts.note: NA is an abbreviation for North American
ta and cheers are both informal British ways of saying thanks

indicators.note: the leader of a word is its first letter

parts.note: the first letter of Lebanese

explanation.surface: An American cheers on the leader of a Lebanese province.
explanation.walkthrough: Natal was a province of South Africa until 1994, now part of KwaZulu-Natal; 'Lebanese' sets a false Middle Eastern trail.
explanation.definitionFit: Natal was a former South African province, so it is a province that existed in the past.

clue.text: Le Pen's horrid spitefulness

indicators.note: horrid suggests something nasty and disordered, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: six letters of fodder, including the possessive S

explanation.surface: The French politician Le Pen shows nasty malice.
explanation.definitionFit: Spleen means bad temper or spite, from the old belief that the organ was the seat of ill humour.

clue.text: Leave Devon river area on time

parts.note: the Exe is a river in Devon, a county in south-west England
A is the abbreviation for area
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: An instruction to depart the Devon river area on schedule.
explanation.walkthrough: An exeat is formal permission for absence, typically a weekend leave from a British boarding school.
explanation.definitionFit: Exeat, Latin for 'let him go out', is a granted leave of absence, matching the noun sense of leave.

clue.text: Englishman down under penning English verse

indicators.note: penning means enclosing as in a pen, so the outer word holds the letter

parts.note: Pom is Australian slang for an English person
E is the abbreviation for English

explanation.surface: An English expat in Australia writes some English poetry.
explanation.walkthrough: Penning looks like writing, which fits verse, but here it means enclosing.
explanation.definitionFit: A poem is a piece of verse, a composition in metrical lines.

clue.text: Awkward writer going back to cut pronoun

indicators.note: to cut into something is to go inside it, so this piece sits within the pronoun

parts.note: it is a pronoun

indicators.note: going back means travelling the other way, so the word is read from right to left

parts.note: a pen is a writing instrument

explanation.surface: A clumsy author returns to edit out a pronoun.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Writer' is the implement, not the author.
explanation.definitionFit: Inept means lacking skill, clumsy, which is the sense of awkward.

clue.text: Penelope mentioned hosting some sort of wedding

indicators.note: hosting means having inside, so the answer is contained within the run of words

parts.note: the letters run across the end of the name and the start of the verb

explanation.surface: Penelope brought up a certain kind of wedding.
explanation.definitionFit: An elopement is a secret marriage after running away, so it is one particular kind of wedding.

clue.text: Murderous Greek woman sent my claret flying

indicators.note: flying suggests things scattering through the air, so the letters land in a new order

parts.note: twelve letters of fodder

explanation.surface: A furious Greek woman knocked my glass of red wine across the room.
explanation.walkthrough: Claret is red Bordeaux wine; the murderess fits a woman hurling wine.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek legend Clytemnestra murdered her husband Agamemnon on his return from Troy.
